title: Text purposes

2026-11-04T17:58:50Z autoreview: cleared with the fix (card wording)

match.reason: The bank point covers only imaginative, persuasive and informative purposes, while the new point also requires reflective and analytical, and it is written for Year 11 rather than Year 7.

draft.title: Text purposes
card: tells a made-up story or creates a world to entertain. It often uses characters, a plot and vivid description.
looks back on a personal experience and thinks about what it meant. It often uses I and shows the writer's feelings.
gives facts so the reader learns something. It uses clear, neutral language and often has headings.
tries to change what the reader thinks or does. It gives a clear opinion and reasons to back it. Analytical texts explain how or why something works, with evidence.
draft.remember: A writer picks structure and language to suit what the text is meant to do.

a.q: Sam writes about the day he moved house. He explains how it felt and what he learned about change. What is the purpose?
opts: Reflective, to think about a personal experience
Informative, to give facts about moving house
Persuasive, to convince readers to move house
Imaginative, to tell a made-up adventure story
a.why: Sam looks back on his own experience and thinks about its meaning, which is reflective. It is not informative, because he is not mainly giving facts for the reader to learn.
a.clue: Is Sam looking back on his own life?

b.q: A school newsletter article has the heading 'Walk to school week'. It says why walking is better than driving and ends by telling families to join in. What is its main purpose?
opts: Persuasive, to get families to take part
Informative, to list facts about the week
Imaginative, to entertain with a story
Reflective, to look back on a past walk
b.why: The article gives reasons and ends with a call to act, so it aims to change what readers do. It has a heading like an informative text, but a heading alone does not decide the purpose.
b.clue: What does the last line ask readers to do?

a.best: Reflective, to think about a personal experience

b.best: Persuasive, to get families to take part

problems.detail: The analytical purpose is tucked into the end of the Persuasive bullet instead of getting its own bullet. Students could read analytical texts as a kind of persuasive text. It needs a separate line, such as 'Analytical: explains how or why something works, using evidence.'

check.summary: Both questions are sound and each has one clear answer. The card puts the analytical definition inside the Persuasive bullet, which could make it seem part of persuasive writing, so it should have its own bullet.

proposal.title: Text purposes
card: An imaginative text tells a made-up story to entertain, using characters and vivid description. A reflective text looks back on a personal experience, often using I, and thinks about what it meant.
An informative text gives facts so the reader learns something. It uses clear, neutral language and often has headings.
A persuasive text tries to change what the reader thinks or does. It gives a clear opinion, reasons to back it and often a call to act.
An analytical text explains how or why something works, using evidence such as examples. Its aim is to explain, not to get the reader to act.
proposal.remember: A writer picks structure and language to suit what the text is meant to do.
